title: Broadcast Nudes

jokes.text: Larry asks to call Hefner 'Hef', then immediately positions it as a mutual intimacy exchange: 'You may. Ok. Call me Larry. Ok, Larry.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks if he can call Hugh Hefner by his famous nickname, which everyone already does
jokes.punchline: Larry then formally offers Hefner permission to call him 'Larry' — as if that's an equivalent trade of intimacy, exposing Larry's oblivious self-importance
jokes.explanation: A quietly precise character joke — Larry performs mutual intimacy with a celebrity as if granting 'Larry' is some privilege equivalent to 'Hef.' It's a small, sharp exposure of Larry's ego through the rhythm of the exchange. Character-specific and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah. We've All seen her.

jokes.text: Larry: 'You don't have any of those test shots with you?' after Hefner explains the centerfold selection process
jokes.setup: Hefner has just described the professional, clinical process by which Playboy selects centerfolds — test shots, promising candidates, etc.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately drops the journalistic facade and asks if Hefner literally brought nude photos to the show — revealing his actual motivation for booking the guest
jokes.explanation: The economy here is excellent — one short question completely deflates the professional interview frame and exposes Larry's voyeuristic wishful thinking. The deadpan delivery and Hefner's flat 'I don't' reply maximizes the comedy of deflation.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Hey is all you need.

jokes.text: Larry says about Hefner's wife/playmate: 'Yeah. We've all seen her.' [Laughter]
jokes.setup: Hefner mentions his wife was a Playmate of the Year; Larry says 'I didn't want to say anything'
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah. We've all seen her.' — delivered casually, the line acknowledges that Larry (like every man) has ogled Hefner's wife in the magazine, undercutting any pretense of decorum
jokes.explanation: Economy is near-perfect — four words, collective confession, laugh track justified. The 'we've all seen her' implicates the entire audience. Brief, honest, funny. A small gem of economy.

jokes.text: Hefner explains meeting his wife: 'I asked her if she wanted to watch a film.' — pause — Larry's silent beat.
jokes.setup: Hefner says they met at the mansion while 'watching a movie'
jokes.punchline: Hefner corrects himself to 'watch a film' — the pretentious word choice from the man who literally runs a softcore empire is absurd; Larry's implied silent acknowledgment seals it
jokes.explanation: Hefner calling it a 'film' instead of 'movie' at the Playboy Mansion is a mild absurdist touch — the euphemism implies it wasn't exactly cinema. Understated and subtle; works better on reread.

dialogue.line: In my bedroom In a box next to my bed, I have every tape Of every playboy after dark Ever made.

jokes.text: Larry: 'You're going to the kitchen to get something from the fridge and bump into Miss January. That's the way it is. And you say, Hey... That's all you need to say because you're Hugh Hefner.'
jokes.setup: Larry is describing Hefner's enviable domestic situation with beautiful women around the mansion
jokes.punchline: 'Hey is all you need.' — Larry's fantasy-narration collapses into envious wonder; the mundane word 'hey' is the peak of his imagination for what Hefner says
jokes.explanation: Larry's riff reveals his own frustrated male fantasy dressed up as host banter. The reduction to 'hey' as Hefner's magic word is the right comic button — simple, envious, self-deflating without Larry realizing it.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: That would be a hoot to Be invited to one of those.

jokes.text: During commercial break, someone tells Hefner: 'You have a little hair there coming down.' — a grooming note to Hugh Hefner.
jokes.setup: The show cuts to a commercial break and the behind-the-scenes production reality kicks in
jokes.punchline: The notoriously glamorous, silk-pajama-wearing Hugh Hefner needs a mundane grooming fix during break — humanizing him comically
jokes.explanation: Mild behind-the-scenes deflation of celebrity mystique. Functional but not especially sharp — the show has done more with this kind of moment elsewhere. A light chuckle at most.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Jesus, did you see how Hank Was all over hefner? He did everything But hump his leg.

jokes.text: A staff member approaches Hefner during break: 'I just want you to know that it's an honor to be this close to you.'
jokes.setup: During the commercial break, a crew member named Frank approaches Hefner
jokes.punchline: Frank's confession — 'it's an honor to be this close to you' — is mortifyingly sincere, suggesting the Hefner mystique extends even to male crew members in an unseemly way
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe moment — the excessive reverence from a random male crew member to Hefner is inherently awkward. Sets up the running joke of male deference to Hefner throughout the episode.

jokes.text: The same crew member (Frank) reveals he has every tape of 'Playboy After Dark' ever made — in a box next to his bed.
jokes.setup: Frank has already said it's an honor to be close to Hefner; now he escalates by confessing to his Hefner tape collection
jokes.punchline: 'In my bedroom, in a box next to my bed' — the specific location (next to the bed, not in a closet or storage) makes this deeply creepy and funny
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'in a box next to my bed' is what elevates this above a simple oversharing joke — it places the collection in the most intimate possible location. Escalates naturally from joke #7.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You could Stand on the roof And watch Angie dickinson Sunbathe.

jokes.text: Hank introduces Darlene to Hefner with a full bio: 'She's from Madison, Wisconsin, and her hobbies include...' — trailing off, clearly hoping Hefner will be interested in her
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to impress Hefner; Hefner asks who Darlene is
jokes.punchline: Hank launches into a dating-show-style introduction of his own colleague, trailing off mid-sentence — it's both obsequious and absurd
jokes.explanation: This is deeply Hank — using Darlene as a commodity to curry favor with Hefner, presenting her like a contestant. The trailing off ('hobbies include...') is the perfect incompletion. Strong character integration for Hank's particular brand of craven showbiz behavior.

jokes.text: Artie to Larry about Hank: 'Jesus, did you see how Hank was all over Hefner? He did everything but hump his leg.'
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry are backstage watching Hank's embarrassing fawning over Hefner
jokes.punchline: 'He did everything but hump his leg.' — Artie's blunt, animalistic metaphor perfectly captures Hank's behavior
jokes.explanation: Artie's line is the episode's first genuinely great joke. It's perfectly calibrated — 'hump his leg' is crude but exact, from a character (Artie) who speaks in old-school, unfiltered producer-speak. Economy is excellent: one image does all the work. Quotable, character-specific, and earns its vulgarity.

dialogue.line: After many years Of trying, Hank Kingsley is going To appear in playboy.

jokes.text: Artie about Carson's house: 'Great house. Yes. You could stand on the roof and watch Angie Dickinson sunbathe.'
jokes.setup: Artie and Larry are agreeing Carson had a wonderful house
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'great house' assessment is immediately followed by its real merit: rooftop sightlines to Angie Dickinson sunbathing — revealing that Artie's architectural appreciation is entirely prurient
jokes.explanation: A brilliant Artie line — his entire architectural enthusiasm is revealed as voyeuristic calculation. The specificity of Angie Dickinson (a real '70s/'80s sex symbol) is perfect period detail. The deadpan delivery of a deeply inappropriate observation as if it were a standard home feature is Artie at his best.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Actually, it's not The interview. It's a feature about women Who work in television.
But, Hank, You're a man.

jokes.text: Larry and Artie debate taking a plant from the set. Larry: 'It's a Mediterranean ficus. It's a very classy plant. Look perfect by your fireplace.' Artie: 'Think so? Yes. No.'
jokes.setup: Larry wants to borrow a plant from the TV set for the Architectural Digest shoot
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately contradicts himself ('Yes. No.') — the beat captures the absurdity of grown men seriously debating plant theft for a magazine photo
jokes.explanation: Mild comedy of the mundane — two powerful TV men debating plant selection. Artie's instant self-contradiction is the funniest beat. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I-i didn't ask, But I would assume, yeah.

jokes.text: Hank announces to Darlene: 'After many years of trying, Hank Kingsley is going to appear in Playboy.' Then: 'Actually, it's not the interview. It's a feature about women who work in television.' Then: 'But, Hank, you're a man. Right, but you're a woman.'
jokes.setup: Hank announces triumphantly that he'll appear in Playboy 'after many years of trying'
jokes.punchline: The reveal that it's a feature about women who work in TV — not the interview he implied — and his response to 'but you're a man' is 'right, but you're a woman,' as if that explains everything
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed three-beat joke. First beat: Hank's grandiose announcement ('many years of trying' for a Playboy appearance is already pathetic). Second beat: the misdirect deflation (it's a women's feature). Third beat: Hank's non-logic ('you're a woman') as if gender is simply tradeable. The escalating humiliation of Hank's ego is character-perfect and structurally tight.

dialogue.line: Your dad's Passed away, right?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: We think so. We're not sure. He left when I was 7.

jokes.text: Hank explains his emotional investment: 'My dad, Henry Kingsley Sr., was a charter subscriber to Playboy.' Then: 'Your dad's passed away, right? We think so. We're not sure. He left when I was 7.'
jokes.setup: Hank is emotionally explaining why appearing in Playboy would make his father proud
jokes.punchline: 'We think so. We're not sure. He left when I was 7.' — the pivot from tender to casually devastating abandonment, delivered without self-pity
jokes.explanation: This is a dark gem. The setup — Hank wants to make his dead father proud — leads to the reveal that they don't even know if he's dead, because he abandoned the family when Hank was 7. The casual delivery of 'he left when I was 7' after 'we think so, we're not sure' is funny AND genuinely sad, which is precisely what The Larry Sanders Show does at its best. Character integration is exceptional — this explains so much about Hank's desperate need for validation.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No bush.

jokes.text: 'Your dad's passed away, right?' / 'We think so. We're not sure. He left when I was 7.'
jokes.setup: Darlene gently checks whether Hank's father has passed — implying the tribute angle is moot if he's alive
jokes.punchline: 'We think so. We're not sure. He left when I was 7.' — Hank's father is not dead, just gone, and the family doesn't even know if he's alive
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. 'We think so. We're not sure. He left when I was 7.' is perfectly structured dark comedy — three beats of escalating revelation delivered with Hank's complete lack of self-awareness. He's just unraveled his entire emotional manipulation in one sentence. The joke recontextualizes everything: the father isn't a dead hero, he's an absent stranger. The economy is exceptional — nine words do devastating character work. Pure Tambor-Hank.

dialogue.line: [Laughs] Yes, in my own 'I can't believe I did it That way myself' way. Yes, I am. I guess.

jokes.text: Artie delivers his note to Hank about the Playboy shoot: 'It'll be very tasteful... No bush.'
jokes.setup: Artie has heard about the Playboy idea and sits Hank down gravely, as if delivering a serious production note
jokes.punchline: 'No bush.' — delivered as a simple, practical production directive, as if it's just another line note
jokes.explanation: Two words. One of the funniest moments in the episode. The structure is perfect: a long, grave wind-up (Artie sits Hank down, all seriousness) followed by a two-word 'note' that is both absurdly specific and completely practical in context. Only Artie can deliver 'No bush' as a production directive with this tone — it's Rip Torn's character distilled to its essence. Maximum economy, total character integration, earned through context. This approaches the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Artie insists on keeping the Playboy shoot 'low profile' because 'Larry Sanders is the star here, goddamn it.'
jokes.setup: Artie is supposedly advising Hank about tasteful presentation
jokes.punchline: His real concern is revealed: not Darlene's dignity or the show's reputation, but Larry's ego and star ranking
jokes.explanation: Artie's protectiveness of Larry's star status — even in the context of a nude magazine feature involving a production assistant — is funny and character-consistent. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Larry tries to ask Francine to move in: 'Yes, in my own I-can't-believe-I-did-it-that-way-myself way. Yes, I am.'
jokes.setup: Francine asks if Larry is asking her to move in; Larry has backed into the invitation through a conversation about an Architectural Digest photo
jokes.punchline: Larry acknowledges the absurdity of his own romantic communication style — he can't even ask someone to move in directly, and his meta-commentary on his own awkwardness is somehow the most awkward possible response
jokes.explanation: Larry's self-aware cringe about his own romantic ineptitude is very much in his character. The hyphenated self-description is funny — he's analyzing his own inadequacy in real time. Strong character integration for Larry's particular brand of emotionally avoidant self-consciousness.

dialogue.speaker: Phil

jokes.text: Francine's concern about moving in: 'I don't want anyone thinking I decorated this house.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Francine are having a semi-serious conversation about moving in together
jokes.punchline: Francine's objection is not about commitment or readiness — it's that she doesn't want to be associated with Larry's taste in home decor
jokes.explanation: The misdirect is sharp — a relationship conversation pivots on interior design vanity. The specificity of the objection (not commitment-phobia, but aesthetic shame) is funny and reveals Francine's character priorities. Clean, well-constructed, and quotable.

jokes.text: Larry defends his house as tasteful; Artie looks around and says: 'What is this? That's a head carved out of rock. This looks like the junior suite in the Four Seasons.'
jokes.setup: Larry is offended that Francine doesn't want people to think she decorated his house
jokes.punchline: Artie's assessment: a 'head carved out of rock' and overall resemblance to a hotel junior suite — the specific, deflating comparison is both accurate and devastating to Larry's self-image
jokes.explanation: The 'junior suite in the Four Seasons' is the right insult — not awful, but generic and status-conscious in a way that indicts Larry's taste perfectly. Artie delivers it as architectural criticism, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Larry's response to 'looks like the junior suite in the Four Seasons': 'Thank you. Jeannie and I met there.'
jokes.setup: Artie has insulted Larry's house by comparing it to a hotel suite
jokes.punchline: Larry takes it as a compliment and reveals he and his ex-wife met at the Four Seasons — making the critique now also an accidental emotional land mine
jokes.explanation: A two-layer joke: Larry mishears an insult as a compliment (layer one), then reveals the sentimental reason he'd take it as one — his failed marriage (layer two). The offhand mention of Jeannie (the ex-wife) adds pathos and shows Larry's emotional arrested development around his divorce. Very Larry Sanders.

dialogue.speaker: Hank

jokes.text: Artie on where to put the African violet: 'In the crapper.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks where Artie thinks a plant should go in the house
jokes.punchline: Artie, who has clearly lost patience with the house's decor, suggests the plant belongs in the bathroom — his contempt expressed through planting advice
jokes.explanation: Artie's dismissive bluntness is always funny. 'The crapper' for an African violet is a properly Artie answer — crude, specific, final. Good economy.

jokes.text: Larry's warning: 'Don't talk that way when the Architectural Digest people are here.'
jokes.setup: Artie has just said 'crapper' in Larry's house
jokes.punchline: Larry's concern is not about Artie's contempt for his house but about propriety in front of the magazine — revealing his priorities: appearance over substance
jokes.explanation: A small character beat — Larry's obsession with how things look to outsiders overrides everything else. Functional, consistent.

jokes.text: Darlene explains she did the test photos: 'There was no one there but me and the photographer.' Others: 'Some slimebag, right?' Darlene: 'No. She seemed nice.' Others: 'She?'
jokes.setup: The men assume the Playboy photographer is a male 'slimebag' — the expected Playboy stereotype
jokes.punchline: The photographer is a woman — the 'She?' reaction beat reveals how completely their assumptions about the Playboy world are gendered
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirect — the female photographer subverts the expected sleazy male Playboy photographer cliché. The men's synchronized 'She?' is a good reaction beat. Economical and structurally sound.

dialogue.speaker: Hank

jokes.text: Darlene: 'Hank really wants me to [do Playboy], and I owe him a lot.' Then the reveal: 'If it wasn't for Hank, I would still be being sawed in half by the Amazing Clifford for two shows a night.'
jokes.setup: Darlene explains she's doing this for Hank because she owes him
jokes.punchline: The debt is revealed: Hank rescued her from being a magician's assistant (being sawed in half by 'the Amazing Clifford' — twice nightly)
jokes.explanation: Wonderful absurdist backstory. 'The Amazing Clifford' is exactly the right name — slightly pompous, slightly sad. 'Two shows a night' adds the professional grind detail that makes it funnier. The specificity of a magician's sawing act as the alternative to Playboy is absurdly perfect and reveals Darlene's limited prior options without being mean about it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Just Larry and me In a decorating magazine? People might get The wrong idea. I would.

jokes.text: Response to Darlene's Amazing Clifford revelation: 'The more I hear about this, it sounds to me like there's little difference between Hank and the Amazing Clifford.' Then: 'Clifford probably dresses better.'
jokes.setup: Someone notes there's little difference between Hank (who found Darlene) and the magician who exploited her
jokes.punchline: 'Clifford probably dresses better.' — a casual, brutal assessment of Hank's sartorial standing relative to a two-bit magician
jokes.explanation: The callback to Clifford is fast and devastating. The suggestion that a magician who saws women in half dresses better than Hank Kingsley is both a character insult and an absurd escalation. The line lands harder because Clifford was just introduced — the callback is almost immediate, which means the joke rewards attentive watching. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You're gonna be disappointed. You'll see.

jokes.text: Writer brings in 'Playboy After Dark' tapes for Larry: 'Pay attention to Mort Sahl. You could learn something.'
jokes.setup: Larry wanted the 'Playboy After Dark' tapes; a writer delivers them
jokes.punchline: The instruction to pay attention to Mort Sahl in a tape from the Playboy mansion implies Larry's interest in the tapes is purely prurient, but someone calls him out by naming the actual comedic content he should study
jokes.explanation: A mild insider joke — Mort Sahl was a genuine comedian on 'Playboy After Dark,' and the suggestion that Larry should study him is a gentle dig at Larry's pretensions about the tapes. Insiders appreciate it more than casual viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Standing Next to Hank, You'll come off Like carl sagan.

jokes.text: Writers reveal they found Darlene's test photos in a big envelope with a Playboy bunny on it: 'We just thought it was a new issue.'
jokes.setup: The writers somehow got hold of Darlene's nude test photos
jokes.punchline: 'We just thought it was a new issue' — their excuse reveals they were actively expecting Playboy to arrive at the office, which is itself the joke
jokes.explanation: Decent joke about TV writers' office culture — the implication that Playboy is a regular delivery item to the writers' room is both funny and probably accurate. The excuse is weak enough to be plausible.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I've got a face That cracks mirrors. That's why I'm a producer.

jokes.text: Larry sees the test photos of Darlene and says sanctimoniously: 'No. No. This is not good. This is not right. This is not our property.' Then beat — clearly looking at them.
jokes.setup: Larry lectures about the impropriety of looking at Darlene's private test photos
jokes.punchline: The pause and '[laughs]' reveal he is absolutely looking at them while delivering the moral lecture — his hypocrisy is the joke
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the gap between Larry's words and actions — he performs moral outrage while clearly ogling. This is proto-Curb territory: a character who can't stop doing what he's criticizing. The structure (righteous speech + visual action contradiction) is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Hank

jokes.text: Hank confronts the writers about stealing the photos; Artie catches Hank yelling the names of men's magazines: 'We're not talking about Hustler or Penthouse or Swank or Juggs or Screw!'
jokes.setup: Hank is outraged that the writers looked at Darlene's photos without permission
jokes.punchline: In defending Playboy's dignity, Hank lists competitor magazines — 'Swank or Juggs or Screw' — the names themselves are the joke, and the escalating absurdity of the list is perfect
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the list — 'Swank or Juggs or Screw' escalates to increasingly disreputable magazine titles, with 'Screw' as the perfect final beat. Hank's indignant defense of Playboy's reputation while listing these titles is pure comic irony. The names themselves are funny.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene

jokes.text: Artie's note to Hank: 'Shouting out the names of some of this country's finest men's publications outside the ladies' crapper is not low profile.'
jokes.setup: Artie told Hank to keep the Playboy situation 'low profile'; Hank has been screaming magazine names in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Artie's callback to the 'low profile' note — delivered with full Artie gravitas — is both a callback and a masterpiece of understatement about what 'not low profile' looks like
jokes.explanation: This is Artie at his most perfectly calibrated. 'This country's finest men's publications' is an absurdly elevated description for Juggs and Screw. 'Outside the ladies' crapper' is the specific location detail that seals it. The callback to 'low profile' pays off beautifully. Economy, character integration, and structure are all high. One of the episode's best lines.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, Hank. It's america's loss.

jokes.text: Bernadette Peters reference: 'Miss Bernadette Peters is down that hallway in her dressing room.' — said as context for why screaming is bad.
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining why Hank's shouting is a problem
jokes.punchline: The fact that Bernadette Peters — a legitimate Broadway/TV star — is apparently just down the hall witnessing this chaos is funny contextually
jokes.explanation: Mild show-business texture joke — a real celebrity is nearby to be embarrassed by this behavior. Works as atmosphere more than as a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Photographer
dialogue.line: Might be fun to get you And Hank on the couch.

jokes.text: Hank suggests maybe a 'weird intern' was shouting — 'That's why they call him the weird intern.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to deflect blame for screaming magazine names in the hallway
jokes.punchline: He blames a 'weird intern' — and then his justification ('that's why they call him the weird intern') is circular logic that admits nothing while explaining everything
jokes.explanation: Hank's deflection and the circular logic of 'that's why they call him the weird intern' is a quick, clean joke about institutional blame-shifting. The absurdist naming of this unnamed character works.

jokes.text: Darlene: 'If you think it's so great, show everyone your tits.'
jokes.setup: Hank has been pressuring Darlene to pose nude as a career move
jokes.punchline: Darlene's blunt, direct challenge — 'show everyone your tits' — turns the exploitation logic directly back on Hank
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that completely puncture Hank's logic and expose the gender dynamic at play. Darlene's sudden directness after being the episode's most passive character is a satisfying character moment. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene

jokes.text: Hank pleading with Darlene not to leave the photo: 'Don't make me sit alone. I'll look like Harvey Korman.'
jokes.setup: Hank wants Darlene in the Architectural Digest photo with him so he has company
jokes.punchline: His fear is looking like Harvey Korman — a specific, industry-insider reference to a famous sidekick who always looked slightly lost without his star (Tim Conway, Carol Burnett)
jokes.explanation: The Harvey Korman reference is pitch-perfect for the show's industry-insider register — Korman was the ultimate second banana, eternally eclipsed. Hank invoking him as his nightmare vision of himself is character gold. Only Hank could frame his existential insecurity through a very specific showbiz analogy. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: There was a small grease fire At the site last night. No, no. It's only Going to push us back About, oh, 10 months.

jokes.text: Hank lays out his romantic strategy: 'This way, you take the picture, then you move in. That's a better way.'
jokes.setup: Hank is explaining the path Larry should use to get Francine to move in
jokes.punchline: Hank has constructed a theory where appearing in Architectural Digest together leads directly to cohabitation — as if the magazine feature is a formal step in a relationship protocol
jokes.explanation: Hank's sincere presentation of a completely backwards relationship logic (magazine shoot → moving in) is funny because he believes it. The confidence is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Those fuckers. Fuckers!

jokes.text: Artie, being slowly drawn into the Architectural Digest photo argument, imagines the shot: 'Wouldn't a picture of me and her look really nice? With your arm around your lady with a big bouquet of baby's breath behind you.' Then snaps back: 'Whoa, horsie, whoa. You got me sucked in for a second.'
jokes.setup: Artie has been refusing to get involved in Larry's relationship/photography drama
jokes.punchline: Artie momentarily gets caught up imagining the domestic scene — even describing it warmly ('your lady,' 'baby's breath') — then catches himself with 'Whoa, horsie, whoa'
jokes.explanation: 'Whoa, horsie, whoa' is a great Artie line — the self-correction is funnier than the setup because Artie's entire character is built on refusing emotional involvement, and here he almost gets caught caring. 'Baby's breath' is the tell — he's gone too far into the domestic fantasy.

jokes.text: Artie exits: 'Brad Pitt's in the green room. I'm going to see if he's as cute as everybody says.' Larry: 'You're gonna be disappointed.'
jokes.setup: Artie is looking for an excuse to exit the uncomfortable relationship conversation
jokes.punchline: Artie, a gruff old-school producer, frames his interest in Brad Pitt's appearance as casual curiosity — the incongruity of Artie going to assess Brad Pitt's hotness is the joke
jokes.explanation: Artie's curiosity about Brad Pitt's looks is funny partly because it's incongruous for the character, and partly because Larry's confident 'You're gonna be disappointed' implies he's already made this assessment himself. Both men casually evaluating Brad Pitt's attractiveness is an unexpected character beat.

jokes.text: 'Brad Pitt's in the green room. I'm going to see if he's as cute as everybody says.' / Larry: 'You're gonna be disappointed. You'll see.'
jokes.setup: Artie exits the argument by announcing he's going to check on Brad Pitt
jokes.punchline: Larry's confident 'You're gonna be disappointed. You'll see.' — Larry dismissing Brad Pitt's attractiveness with complete conviction, which reads as petty jealousy dressed as sage advice
jokes.explanation: Larry's dismissal of Brad Pitt — specifically 'You'll see' — is perfect insecure-host comedy. The confidence of the claim (this man who is objectively handsome will disappoint you) reveals Larry's fragile ego. A classic Larry Sanders bit in miniature.

jokes.text: Artie to Darlene about standing next to Hank: 'Standing next to Hank, you'll come off like Carl Sagan.'
jokes.setup: Darlene is worried she'll look stupid in the Playboy photo
jokes.punchline: Artie assures her that standing next to Hank will make anyone look like an intellectual giant — specifically Carl Sagan, the astronomer famous for being brilliant and accessible
jokes.explanation: Carl Sagan is the perfect choice — not just 'smart person' but specifically the most famously accessible, beloved public intellectual of the era. The implication that anyone next to Hank would achieve that elevation is a devastatingly precise Hank insult delivered as reassurance. Economy is excellent; character integration (this is pure Artie) is very high.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I've never told many people this, but I knew Marilyn Monroe. We were friends.' Then: 'She was very self-conscious till she learned how to use her beauty as an asset.'
jokes.setup: Artie is giving Darlene a pep talk about posing for Playboy
jokes.punchline: Artie casually drops that he was personal friends with Marilyn Monroe as if this is a normal thing — the specificity and casualness of the claim (and his advice based on it) is both funny and characterizes Artie as someone from a genuinely different Hollywood era
jokes.explanation: The Marilyn Monroe friendship is quintessential Artie — it's exactly the kind of anecdote only Artie could have, and it's delivered not as a brag but as a practical reference point for advice. The show uses Artie's age and history brilliantly, and this is a strong example. Character integration is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: Artie's self-description: 'I've got a face that cracks mirrors. That's why I'm a producer.'
jokes.setup: Artie is explaining to Darlene why she should use her looks — contextualizing it against his own situation
jokes.punchline: 'I've got a face that cracks mirrors. That's why I'm a producer.' — the self-deprecating logic (ugliness → behind-the-scenes career) is both funny and oddly wise
jokes.explanation: This is a great line. The internal logic — ugly face → producer, because the entertainment industry puts beautiful people in front of the camera and everyone else behind it — is delivered with zero self-pity and absolute conviction. It's funny, self-aware, true about the industry, and completely Artie. Economy is exceptional. This approaches the 8.0 anchor in quality.

jokes.text: Artie's final pep talk note: 'If you're going to do this, do it for yourself and no one else. Especially not for fucking Hank.'
jokes.setup: Artie is giving Darlene earnest advice about her decision
jokes.punchline: The 'especially not for fucking Hank' addition — delivered with genuine feeling — turns a sincere moment into a Hank insult, suggesting Artie's real message is simply anti-Hank
jokes.explanation: The addition of 'especially not for fucking Hank' to otherwise decent advice is very funny — it reveals Artie's underlying agenda and is a perfect button. The word 'fucking' before 'Hank' (not a generic f-word) is character-perfect Artie contempt.

jokes.text: Darlene: 'They hated my test shots, didn't they?' Hank: 'Oh, those fuckers! Those fuckers! Bunch of sleazebags, every one of them.'
jokes.setup: Darlene realizes the real reason the Playboy piece was cancelled is her photos weren't good enough
jokes.punchline: Hank's over-the-top outrage on Darlene's behalf is transparently self-serving — he's not defending her dignity, he's furious that his concept was rejected. The curse-laden righteousness is disproportionate and funny.
jokes.explanation: Hank's impotent rage against Playboy is funny, but the joke is fairly predictable at this point — we know Hank's self-interest drives his apparent loyalty. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: Hank: 'What did they say about me?' Darlene: 'About you? Oh, they loved you. They want to know if you're interested in doing a... pictorial alone.'
jokes.setup: Hank asks what Playboy said about him specifically
jokes.punchline: Darlene reveals Playboy wants Hank to do a nude solo pictorial — the implication being they want to publish nude photos of Hank Kingsley, which is horrifying and absurd
jokes.explanation: The reversal is well-constructed — Darlene gets revenge by lying to Hank that Playboy wants HIM to pose nude. The pause before 'pictorial alone' is a good structural beat. The absurdity of Hank Kingsley in a Playboy pictorial is the joke's core.

jokes.text: Darlene: 'I am interested, Hank. I'll do it for me, not for you. But for me, I want to do it.'
jokes.setup: Darlene has just told Hank that Playboy wants him; now she reverses her earlier position
jokes.punchline: Darlene uses Artie's exact empowerment language ('do it for yourself, not for anyone else') while clearly just screwing with Hank — the feminist framing is weaponized for pettiness, which is perfect
jokes.explanation: This is a satisfying callback to Artie's pep talk — Darlene has absorbed the language of self-determination and is now using it to gaslight Hank. The irony (she's doing the opposite of what she says) is pointed and character-consistent.

jokes.text: Hank's response to Darlene saying she'll pose alone: 'Ok. Here's what we'll do. Uh, you'll call them and say to them, Look, I am not going to do a pictorial unless Hank Kingsley is part of it.'
jokes.setup: Darlene has just said she'll do the pictorial alone, for herself
jokes.punchline: Hank immediately pivots to making Darlene's solo empowerment into leverage for his own inclusion — the speed of his self-interest is the joke
jokes.explanation: Hank's negotiating position — threatening to withhold Darlene's compliance unless he's included — is perfectly backwards and pathetically Hank. He has no leverage and doesn't realize it. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Hank's real reason for needing publicity: 'My restaurant's opening in less than two months... If I don't get publicity, you know who'll be at the gala opening? You, me, the creditors, and that's it.'
jokes.setup: Hank is explaining why the Playboy publicity was so important to him
jokes.punchline: The restaurant scheme is revealed, and the 'gala opening' attended only by 'you, me, the creditors' is a perfect image of Hank's financial precariousness dressed up in event-planner language
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'you, me, the creditors' is excellent — the creditors attend the gala as guests of honor by necessity. This is a good dark joke about Hank's financial delusion wrapped in showbiz aspiration.

jokes.text: Hank's solution: 'I could wear a Hank's Look Around Café T-shirt.' Darlene: 'You see, it's very hard to pose nude and wear a T-shirt at the same time. In fact, it's downright impossible.'
jokes.setup: Hank suggests a way to get publicity for his restaurant via the nude photo shoot
jokes.punchline: Darlene points out the logical impossibility of wearing a T-shirt while posing nude — the observation is technically obvious but delivered as if it requires explanation
jokes.explanation: The absurd specificity of the restaurant name ('Hank's Look Around Café') is funny, and Darlene's logical observation — 'it's downright impossible' — delivered as if this needs articulating is good deadpan. The escalation from grandiose plan to physical impossibility is clean.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Great. I've become pissy.' — said with resignation about his own mood shift.
jokes.setup: Hank has been outmaneuvered and humiliated
jokes.punchline: 'I've become pissy' — Hank's self-diagnosis of his emotional state, delivered as a factual observation about himself
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly self-aware without being truly self-aware — Hank notices his mood has shifted but doesn't interrogate why. 'Pissy' is the exact right word for Hank's particular brand of petulant sulking. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Artie, they cut me out, those cocksuckers.' Artie laughs: 'Oh, I'm sorry, Hank. It's America's loss.'
jokes.setup: Hank is reporting that Playboy cut him from the feature
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'It's America's loss' — delivered with barely concealed amusement — frames Hank's Playboy rejection as a national tragedy, which is the most perfectly calibrated mock-sympathy possible
jokes.explanation: Great Artie line. 'It's America's loss' is exactly the right register — patriotic, solemn, and utterly ridiculous in context. The laugh before the line (Artie has to suppress it) makes it funnier. Economy is very high. One of Artie's best in the episode.

jokes.text: Hank desperately trying to get Artie to be in the Architectural Digest photo: 'Come on, it's just one little picture. What difference does it make?'
jokes.setup: Hank is now trying to recruit Artie as a substitute photo companion since Darlene and Larry won't cooperate
jokes.punchline: The desperation is the joke — Hank is now willing to put literally anyone in the photo with him to avoid looking like Harvey Korman alone
jokes.explanation: Functional escalation of Hank's desperation — he's cycling through candidates for the photo. Less funny than the Harvey Korman setup, more of a connective tissue beat.

jokes.text: Artie's reaction to the idea of appearing in Architectural Digest with Larry: 'Just Larry and me in a decorating magazine? People might get the wrong idea. I would.'
jokes.setup: Hank suggests Artie join the photo shoot
jokes.punchline: 'People might get the wrong idea. I would.' — Artie not only predicts the misinterpretation but admits he himself would draw the same conclusion about two men in a decorating magazine, which is both homophobic in period-accurate way and self-aware
jokes.explanation: The 'I would' is the crucial addition — Artie doesn't just note what others might think; he admits to the same inference himself. The self-inclusion makes it funnier and more honest. Economy is strong; the joke lands in five words after the setup.

jokes.text: Larry's girlfriend is now in the photo: Artie directing the photographer — 'Max, with this lighting, I'd use an f-8 stop.' Then Hank arrives uninvited and is immediately invited into the shot over Larry's objections.
jokes.setup: Larry has finally gotten Francine to agree to be in the photo; it's a private moment
jokes.punchline: Hank shows up, gets invited in by the photographer, and Larry's objections are immediately overridden — Hank ends up in the photo Larry didn't want him in, just as he ended up being in everything he tries to exclude Hank from
jokes.explanation: A satisfying structural joke — Hank's inescapability is the visual gag. Larry's helpless 'I don't want him in the picture' being overridden by group momentum is a good bit, though more situational than verbal.

jokes.text: Artie to Larry about Hank: 'Might be fun to get you and Hank on the couch.' / Larry: 'I don't want him in the picture.' / Multiple voices: 'Come on, Larry... the more the merrier.' / Larry: 'I don't want him in—' / 'It's just a little picture.'
jokes.setup: Hank has crashed the photo shoot; the photographer suggests including him
jokes.punchline: Larry's protests are steamrolled by everyone — including Artie, who moments ago refused any involvement — through the sheer momentum of the situation
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the reversal — Artie, who refused to be in the picture, now enthusiastically promotes Hank's inclusion without acknowledging the inconsistency. Larry's helpless repeated protests ('I don't want him in—') are an effective cringe escalation.

jokes.text: Photographer's direction: 'Ok, everybody. Say, Hey, now.'
jokes.setup: The Architectural Digest photo shoot is finally happening with everyone crowded together
jokes.punchline: 'Hey, now' is Hank's catchphrase — so the photographer has unknowingly (or knowingly) given Hank the ultimate victory: his catchphrase as the final word of the shoot
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best structural joke. The photographer uses 'Hey, now' — Hank's signature catchphrase — as the photo-direction equivalent of 'Say cheese.' Whether intentional or accidental within the fiction, it's a perfect closing button on the whole photo subplot. Hank gets his moment via his catchphrase as the literal final instruction. Economy is nearly perfect. The callback to the show's running Hank gag earns a rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: 'Love, Darlene.' — the caption/dedication under the photo, presumably on a signed copy.
jokes.setup: The Architectural Digest shoot has concluded, apparently with unexpected warmth
jokes.punchline: The signed dedication 'Love, Darlene' under what was supposed to be a Larry/Francine lifestyle feature is an absurdist button — the production assistant has somehow become the emotional center of the photo
jokes.explanation: A small, odd beat — the signed 'Love, Darlene' implies she's signed the photo as if she's the star, which is a funny reversal of the original intent. Subtle.

jokes.text: Larry and Artie react to the Architectural Digest feature: 'This is fucking bad timing that Darlene's article came out the same day as yours. Otherwise, everyone would be bent over your desk instead of Darlene's.'
jokes.setup: Larry's Architectural Digest feature has come out the same day as Darlene's Playboy pictorial
jokes.punchline: Artie frames everyone's attention to Darlene's naked photos as being literally 'bent over' her desk — a vivid physical image that captures the newsroom's prurient distraction while also accidentally being a decent Architectural Digest vs. Playboy metaphor
jokes.explanation: Artie's frank assessment of male behavior in the office — 'bent over your desk instead of Darlene's' — is vivid and funny, with the added irony that Larry should be grateful Architectural Digest even competes with Playboy for his staff's attention.

jokes.text: Larry about the Architectural Digest issue: 'It's nothing special. You see one, you've seen them all. But how many houses do you see like this?'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to be dismissive of Darlene's Playboy while talking up his own Architectural Digest
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'you see one, you've seen them all' about Playboy immediately followed by his genuine excitement about Architectural Digest — the priorities are completely inverted from what a normal person would say
jokes.explanation: Larry's affected dismissal of Playboy ('you see one, you've seen them all') while eagerly promoting his home magazine is a good character moment — he's trying to maintain dignity while clearly stung by the attention Darlene is getting.

jokes.text: Larry looking at Darlene's Playboy: 'These lilies on the coffee table — that's a sexy touch.'
jokes.setup: Larry is supposedly dismissive of Darlene's Playboy pictorial
jokes.punchline: Despite claiming not to be interested, Larry is clearly scrutinizing the pictorial in detail — commenting on the flower arrangement in a nude photo shoot
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in what Larry focuses on — the lilies, not Darlene — which could mean he's truly a decor obsessive, or that he's too embarrassed to mention what he's actually looking at. Either reading is funny. The 'sexy touch' comment on flowers is a good small joke.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I didn't even know she owned a motorcycle.' — reacting to something in the Playboy spread.
jokes.setup: Larry is going through Darlene's Playboy pictorial
jokes.punchline: The detail of a motorcycle in the shoot is funny — it implies a Playboy 'Girl Next Door' shoot with props Larry didn't know existed in Darlene's life, and his fascination with the motorcycle rather than the naked person is a good character beat
jokes.explanation: A good small joke — Larry's focus on the motorcycle prop reveals either his genuine curiosity about Darlene or his attempt to discuss the pictorial at arm's length. The line 'I didn't even know she owned a motorcycle' has good economy and is a nice oblique way to indicate he's studying the photos.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I've already signed yours.' — implying he already autographed Larry's Architectural Digest copy, unsolicited.
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are looking at each other's respective magazine features
jokes.punchline: Artie has pre-signed Larry's Architectural Digest as if he's a contributing celebrity — the casual presumption that his signature would be wanted is funny
jokes.explanation: Quick and good — Artie's presumption in signing Larry's magazine (without being asked) is a funny small character beat. His ego in assuming the signature is wanted is classic Artie.

jokes.text: Darlene tells Hank: 'I wore the Hank's Look Around Café T-shirt in the main shot. It's a little ripped, but you can still read it.'
jokes.setup: Hank earlier wanted publicity for his restaurant through the Playboy shoot
jokes.punchline: Darlene actually wore the restaurant T-shirt in the nude Playboy shoot — it's 'a little ripped' (i.e., torn open for the nude photo, not accidentally damaged), and she presents this as a genuine favor
jokes.explanation: This is a superb callback and one of the episode's best jokes. The earlier joke established that wearing a T-shirt while posing nude was 'downright impossible.' Darlene's solution — wearing a ripped T-shirt in the nude shot — is both a perfect callback and reveals that the 'ripped' is a euphemism for 'torn open.' The line 'you can still read it' is the perfect button. Structure, callback execution, originality, and earned-vs-cheap are all high. This earns its score.

jokes.text: Darlene informs Hank casually: 'I guess you didn't hear there was a small grease fire at the site last night. No, no. It's only going to push us back about, oh, 10 months.'
jokes.setup: Hank needed the Playboy publicity for his restaurant opening in two months
jokes.punchline: A grease fire has pushed the opening back 10 months — the promotional campaign was irrelevant, the restaurant is in shambles, and Darlene delivers this information with the same tone as a weather update
jokes.explanation: The grease fire revelation retroactively renders all of Hank's scheming — the Playboy negotiation, the t-shirt, the creditor panic — completely pointless. The comic structure of 10 months vs. 2 months is a perfect escalation of futility. 'Oh, 10 months' with the casual pause is a great deadpan delivery note.

jokes.text: Hank, responding to the restaurant T-shirt news, then delivers: 'Very nice.' — and then immediately: 'I guess you didn't hear there was a small grease fire at the site last night. No, no. It's only going to push us back about, oh, 10 months.'
jokes.setup: Darlene has just told Hank about the T-shirt in the Playboy shoot — good news for the restaurant
jokes.punchline: Immediately after 'very nice,' Hank drops the news of the restaurant fire and ten-month delay — the timing is brutal; Darlene's sacrifice is immediately made irrelevant by Hank's disaster
jokes.explanation: The pacing here is excellent — 'Very nice' as a beat before the grease fire revelation lands perfectly. The 10-month delay renders Darlene's heroic T-shirt gesture entirely meaningless, which is darkly funny. Good structural comedy: a gift immediately voided.

jokes.text: Hank sees the Architectural Digest issue and shouts 'Those fuckers! Fuckers!' while Artie calls from off: 'Low profile, Hank!' and Hank continues: 'Bunch of fuckers!'
jokes.setup: Hank has apparently been cropped out of the Architectural Digest photo despite being in the shot
jokes.punchline: Hank's explosion, immediately followed by Artie's 'Low profile, Hank!' callback — the running gag on low profile is the episode's final joke, and Hank responding to the note by continuing to shout 'Bunch of fuckers!' is the perfect button
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke is structurally perfect. It's a triple callback: the 'low profile' running gag, Hank's repeated professional humiliations (Playboy cut, now Architectural Digest crop), and Hank's inability to control himself. Artie's off-camera 'Low profile, Hank!' arriving precisely as Hank screams is textbook sitcom button work. The final 'Bunch of fuckers!' ignoring Artie's note is the perfect last word. High character integration — only Hank could make this ending work, and only Artie could deliver that callback with this timing.

tmdb_overview: Hank manipulates Darlene into agreeing to do a Playboy spread and Larry worries about appearing in Architectural Digest.
